opening.spoken: This record covers the claimed solution of Erdős problem #731: what has been claimed, what it rests on, and what would have to be checked by whom.

short_version.spoken: Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa and Straus asked for a reasonable function f(n) such that, for almost all n, the least m not dividing the central binomial coefficient is asymptotic to f(n). In June 2026 Eric Li posted a paper, and in July a Lean development, resolving the problem under an explicit dyadic-regularity reading of 'reasonable': a best deterministic scale exists for tightness in density, and no dyadically regular f gives the asymptotic equivalence asked for. Whether that reading answers the problem as posed is a judgment a number theorist has to make. Everything here is open.

what_happened.spoken: The claim was pinned from the public record: the problem page, the proof-claims thread, and every artifact the claimants made public, by commit or hash. Nothing was run. A reading guide now lays the claimant's formal statements beside the problem as posed, definition by definition. It finds that the least non-divisor and the density notion are the problem's own, that the third-party formal statement places no condition on the answer and so cannot serve as a reference, and that one difference could change what the claim answers: the claimant's own, openly stated reading of the word reasonable.

do_not_rely_on.spoken: the claimed solution as settled; nothing in it has standing yet

certainty_statement.spoken: Nothing is certified or accepted. Every item is open.

cycles.spoken: Eric Li posted the paper on arXiv; the Erdős-problems AI wiki listed it as a candidate full solution, marked unverified, on June 27. The proof claim was listed on the problem page with links to the paper and a formalisation. The Lean repository's current commit and the paper's second version were posted the same day. The problem page lists one proof claim, not marked accepted by the site.

preregistered.question: Can the open semantic gaps (EG2, and EG4 on the formalisation of 'reasonable') be made cheaper for a human reviewer: the problem as posed, the third-party and the claimant's formal statements, every definition behind them, a plain rendering, and the points to confirm? Is there a meaning-changing difference beyond the one the claimant discloses?
preregistered.rule: Statements quoted verbatim from files fetched read-only at the pinned commits, with file and line; renderings marked as the agent's; every discrepancy recorded whether harmless or not, an undisclosed meaning-changing one opened as an anomaly; worked examples written for Lean and stated as unrun until run; standing unchanged by construction.
predictions: P1: the claimant's A is formal-conjectures' leastNonDivisor (m = 0 excluded) and its density notion is the standard one
P2: the formal-conjectures statement cannot serve as a machine reference (no condition on the answer, positive form); the meaning question concentrates in EG4
P3: dyadic regularity leaves out functions a reader might call reasonable, whose logarithm moves by a bounded amount within a block; rated uncertain, recorded against EG4, no anomaly since disclosed
P4: at least three boundary conventions need a sentence; none changes the meaning
P5: the positive half is tightness in density, weaker than an asymptotic, and supplies no f with A ~ f

misses: P3 named n^α as an excluded reasonable function; it is beside the point, since A(n) = exp((log n)^(1/2+o(1))) for almost all n and no power of n could be an equivalent. The excluded functions that matter are F(n) times a bounded swing inside each block.
Not foreseen: the development also proves inherited oscillation (any working f must swing by a fixed factor inside every block), which narrows the open question to smooth swinging functions.

cycles.spoken: Nervous Machine wrote the reading guide for the question on this record that a machine cannot settle: whether the claim's Lean statements answer the problem Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa and Straus posed. The third-party formal statement turned out not to be usable as a reference, because it places no condition on the answer, so the guide reads the claimant's own statements against the problem page, traces every symbol to its definition with file and line, and writes seventeen small Lean examples that have not yet been run, since nobody has built the development. The least non-divisor and the density notion are the problem's own. One difference could change what the claim answers, and the claimant states it openly: the word reasonable is taken to mean a function whose logarithm is nearly constant on each doubling block, which leaves out smooth functions that swing by a fixed factor inside a block. The readings are the system's, not a mathematician's, so nothing changed standing. A number theorist can now sign or refuse five lines, one of which is that single judgment.

background.spoken: For an integer n let A(n) be the least m that does not divide the central binomial coefficient (2n choose n). The authors say it is not hard to show that for almost all n, A(n) is exp((log n)^(1/2 + o(1))). The problem asks for a reasonable function f(n) with A(n) asymptotic to f(n) for almost all n.

background.spoken: The claim resolves the problem under an explicit dyadic-regularity formalisation of 'reasonable'. On each dyadic block it gives a scale F and proves two-sided tail bounds in natural density around it, so that log A(n) minus the main terms is tight in density, while no dyadically regular deterministic scale satisfies the requested asymptotic equivalence. The author presents this as a two-part answer: F is the best possible deterministic scale, and the equivalence as literally asked cannot hold for any dyadically regular f.
